warmup.q: A Vert.x HTTP handler wraps its 500 ms database call in vertx.executeBlocking(() -> db.lookup()). Four requests arrive at the same moment on a server with one event loop. Roughly how long until all four are answered?
options: About 500 ms: the four lookups run in parallel on the worker pool
About 2,000 ms: by default executeBlocking runs calls from the same context one after another
About 500 ms, but only if the worker pool has at least 4 threads
It never finishes: executeBlocking deadlocks on a single event loop
warmup.why: executeBlocking is ordered by default, and all requests to one HTTP server share its context. The event loop is free, but the four lookups queue behind each other in the back office. This lesson's demo measured 2,012 ms ordered and 511 ms with executeBlocking(callable, false). The default worker pool has 20 threads, so the pool size isn't the limit.

opening:
Picture our post office once more. The clerks from Netty still sit behind the wall, each with a row of boxes, but the manager has added desks: a weighing desk, a price desk, a lost-property desk. Each desk has its own drawers, and the same clerk always serves it, one job at a time. Desks pass notes to each other through labeled mail tubes. Slow jobs go to the back office.

That post office is Vert.x, a toolkit for network programs that runs on Netty's event loops. Here is its surprise. A desk sends four slow jobs to a back office with twenty idle workers, and the answers still come back one at a time.

The trap is easy to fall into, because the obvious fix, sending slow jobs to the back office, looks finished: the warnings stop and the tests pass. Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks finished our tour of Netty. In this lesson, we'll see which clerk serves each desk, send notes through the tubes, meet a floor manager, and find out why the back office works in single file. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a post office of desks, each served by one clerk, with mail tubes between them and a back office for slow jobs. Vert.x names them: contexts on Netty's event loops, verticles, the event bus and executeBlocking. The floor manager reports long calls, and false keeps the back office from working in single file.

Now search your own Vert.x code for executeBlocking( with a single argument, and ask whether those calls really need to wait for each other.

Next, we'll meet Quarkus, a framework that runs on these same clerks. How does it decide, for each job, between the counter clerk, the back office and a cheap temporary helper?

sections.h: One desk, one clerk: a Vert.x context on Netty's event loop
sections.html:
Start with what's underneath. Vert.x 5.2.3, the version this track uses, runs on Netty 4.2.20. When you call Vertx.vertx(), it starts a group of Netty event loops, the clerks from lesson 3. An event loop is one thread, a single line of work inside your program, that watches many connections and runs their code one piece at a time. Vert.x starts two per core by default, 8 on a 4-core machine, named vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 and up. A stack trace later in this lesson ends in io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run, the same loop class Netty uses.

So what does Vert.x add? Rules about who runs your code. The central one is the context: the home of a piece of code, which decides the thread that runs it. Most contexts are event-loop contexts, each tied to one event loop for life. In the post office, a context is the card on a desk that names its clerk.

When you register a handler, Vert.x remembers the current context, and every call of that handler runs there. A handler, in Vert.x, is any piece of your code that Vert.x calls when something happens: a request arrives, a timer fires, a note comes through a tube. The Vert.x docs make a promise about it. A handler is never executed concurrently, and, worker verticles aside, it always runs on the same event loop thread.

That promise is lesson 3's Netty rule, one channel and one loop, stretched over all your code: handlers for HTTP (the protocol of the web), timers and event-bus consumers alike. One clerk serves the desk, one job at a time, so nobody needs to lock the drawers. A field that only one context touches needs no synchronized.

The promise has a price you already know. While a handler runs, its clerk does nothing else, so every desk and every connection on that loop waits. We'll meet the floor manager who watches for that in the last section.

The second change is the API. A future is an object that will hold a result later; you attach code to it, and that code runs when the result arrives. Vert.x 4 offered two styles side by side: callbacks, where you pass a function into the call itself, and futures. Vert.x 5 kept only futures. Every asynchronous method returns an io.vertx.core.Future, and the callback versions are gone:

Java
// Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future
server.listen(8080).onSuccess(s -> System.out.println("listening on " + s.actualPort()));
// Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles:
// server.listen(8080, ar -> ...)  ->  error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface
Kotlin
// Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future
server.listen(8080).onSuccess { s -> println("listening on ${s.actualPort()}") }
// Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles:
// server.listen(8080) { ar -> ... }   the only two-argument listen left is listen(int, String)

The Java error looks unrelated. The compiler, trying to help, found the one two-argument listen that's left, listen(int, String), and complained that a String isn't a lambda. The same change replaced executeBlocking(promise -> ...) with a version that takes a Callable and returns a Future, which the last section puts to work.

A context is the home of your code. Everything registered on it runs on its thread, one task at a time.

A context needs something to belong to. In Vert.x, that something is usually a verticle.

try.title: Hit the Vert.x 5 API change
steps: In ContextsDemo.java, add one line after Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx();: vertx.createHttpServer().listen(8080, ar -> {});.
Predict whether it compiles. Then run the demo with the command below.
try.expect: Compilation fails with error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface. The callback version of listen no longer exists in Vert.x 5, so javac tries listen(int, String) and can't turn your lambda into a String.

sections.h: Desks you deploy: verticles and their threading models
sections.html:
A verticle is a class you deploy into Vert.x, and deploying it gives each instance its own context. It's a desk: a small, self-contained unit with its own drawers (its fields), its own handlers, and the card that names its clerk.

In Vert.x 5 you extend VerticleBase and return a Future from start(), so the deployment finishes only when your setup has. Here is a first weighing desk. It listens at the address desk.weigh and answers every parcel with a JsonObject, Vert.x's map of named values, that says it was accepted. This lesson's lab makes it stricter:

Java
public class WeighingDesk extends VerticleBase {
    @Override
    public Future<?> start() {
        return vertx.eventBus().<JsonObject>consumer("desk.weigh", msg ->
                msg.reply(new JsonObject().put("status", "ACCEPTED"))
        ).completion();                                  // done when the consumer is registered
    }
}

vertx.deployVerticle(WeighingDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));
Kotlin
class WeighingDesk : VerticleBase() {
    override fun start(): Future<*> =
        vertx.eventBus().consumer<JsonObject>("desk.weigh") { msg ->
            msg.reply(JsonObject().put("status", "ACCEPTED"))
        }.completion()                                   // done when the consumer is registered
}

vertx.deployVerticle(::WeighingDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

Read it from the bottom. We deploy two instances, so we pass a factory, a function that makes a new object each time, because each instance must be its own object. In 5.2.3 that factory is a Supplier, though the docs still say Callable. Each instance gets its own event-loop context, usually on different loops, which is how one verticle class uses several cores. Inside one instance, code never runs on two threads at once, so its fields need no locks.

Inside start(), the desk registers a consumer, a handler for notes that arrive at one address. Then it returns completion(), a future that completes once the consumer is registered, and Vert.x waits for it before it calls the deployment done.

Not every desk wants an event-loop clerk. The threading model in DeploymentOptions decides what kind of context a verticle gets. ContextsDemo deploys one verticle of each kind and prints where its start() runs:

[EVENT_LOOP] start() on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=true workerCtx=false
[WORKER] start() on vert.x-worker-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=true
[VIRTUAL_THREAD] start() on vert.x-virtual-thread-0 (virtual) eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=false

EVENT_LOOP, the default, must never block. A WORKER verticle runs on the worker pool, a bounded pool of ordinary threads that are allowed to block, 20 of them by default. It still never runs on two threads at once, but one call can land on a different worker thread from the last. VIRTUAL_THREAD is new in Vert.x 5 and needs Java 21. The verticle runs on virtual threads, cheap threads that the JDK parks while they wait, and future.await() parks the virtual thread until the result arrives.

A virtual-thread verticle also runs one task at a time, with one catch from the docs. A field you read before an await() may have changed after it, because another task of the same verticle can run while you wait.

Here the desk picture breaks a little. A real desk keeps the same clerk all day. A worker desk can get a different clerk from the pool for each job, though never two at once, so it's single-threaded without being tied to one thread.

Each verticle instance is one desk with one context. For more cores, deploy more instances.

Desks need a way to talk without opening each other's drawers. That's the event bus.

try.title: Where does each desk run?
steps: Open ContextsDemo.java (or ContextsDemo.kt). It deploys one verticle per threading model, then calls executeBlocking from an event-loop context.
Predict the thread name in each line, and on which thread onSuccess runs after executeBlocking.

One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ public class ContextsDemo { static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); Context c = Vertx.currentContext(); return t.getName() + (t.isVirtual() ? " (virtual)" : "") + " eventLoopCtx=" + c.isEventLoopContext() + " workerCtx=" + c.isWorkerContext(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + " (cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + "), default worker pool: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); for (ThreadingModel model : List.of(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { await(vertx.deployVerticle(new VerticleBase() { @Override public Future<?> start() { System.out.println("[" + model + "] start() on " + where()); return Future.succeededFuture(); } }, new DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model))); } vertx.runOnContext(v -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()) .onSuccess(name -> System.out.println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on " + name + ", onSuccess runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()))); Thread.sleep(300); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: The first line reports 8 event loops on 4 CPUs and a worker pool of 20. The three verticles start on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0, vert.x-worker-thread-0 and a virtual thread, vert.x-virtual-thread-0. The executeBlocking callable runs on a worker thread, and onSuccess runs back on an event-loop thread: the context that made the call.

sections.h: Notes through the tubes: request, reply and publish on the event bus
sections.html:
The event bus is how verticles talk without sharing objects. There's one per Vertx instance, and an address is just a string, such as desk.weigh. In the post office, it's the system of mail tubes between desks, each tube labeled with a name. You can send a note in three ways:

  • send(address, msg): to one consumer at that address, chosen in turn (round-robin).
  • request(address, msg): to one consumer, and you get a Future of its reply.
  • publish(address, msg): to every consumer at that address.

EventBusDemo deploys two instances of a greeter desk and sends it four requests. Then it tries three addresses: one with nobody behind it, one that fails on purpose, and one that never answers:

request greet #0 -> hello dev0 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1
request greet #1 -> hello dev1 from instance#2 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0
request greet #2 -> hello dev2 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1
request nobody -> NO_HANDLERS code=-1 message=No handlers for address nobody
request fail -> RECIPIENT_FAILURE code=42 message=boom from instance#1
request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> TIMEOUT after 308 ms

The two instances took turns, each on its own loop: the round-robin at work. After them come the three ways a request can fail, each delivered as a ReplyException with a failureType(). NO_HANDLERS means nobody listens at the address, a tube that leads to an empty room. RECIPIENT_FAILURE means the consumer called msg.fail(code, text), and you get its code and text. TIMEOUT means no reply came in time.

The silent consumer deserves a second look. It took the note and never wrote back, and the requester only found out because it had set a timeout of 300 ms. The default is 30 seconds, a long time to stand at a tube. Set one on every request with new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(...).

The reply comes back on the requester's context, not the consumer's. A worker verticle that sends a request handles the reply on a worker thread, and a virtual-thread verticle resumes on its virtual thread. So the promise of one desk and one clerk holds at both ends of a tube.

Two properties keep the event bus from being a message store. First, delivery is best effort: there's no saved copy and no retry, and the docs tell you to write consumers that can safely see the same message twice. Second, inside one JVM a message can be handed over by reference. A codec is the code that turns a message into bytes and back. With a custom local codec whose transform returns its argument, the consumer receives the very object you sent.

Here the tube picture breaks. A real tube carries the sheet away, while this one can leave the same sheet in both hands. Never change a message after you send it. Built-in codecs cover strings, numbers, Buffer, JsonObject and JsonArray; other types need a codec you register.

The event bus carries quick notes between desks. Set a timeout on every request, and treat delivery as best effort.

Notes, timers and requests all run on the clerks. So what happens when one of those jobs doesn't come back?

steps: Open EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Predict which instance answers each of the four requests, and how many lines publish prints.
Change the silent request's timeout from 300 to 1,000 ms and run again. What changes, and what doesn't?

import io.vertx.core.eventbus.EventBus; import io.vertx.core.eventbus.ReplyException; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Point-to-point, publish/subscribe and the three ways a request can fail. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final AtomicInteger IDS = new AtomicInteger(); public static class Greeter extends VerticleBase { final int id = IDS.incrementAndGet(); @Override public Future<?> start() { EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); eb.<String>consumer("greet", m -> m.reply("hello " + m.body() + " from instance#" + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName())); eb.<String>consumer("news", m -> System.out.println(" [news] instance#" + id + " got '" + m.body() + "'")); eb.<String>consumer("fail", m -> m.fail(42, "boom from instance#" + id)); return eb.<String>consumer("silent", m -> { /* never replies */ }).completion(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); await(vertx.deployVerticle(Greeter::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) System.out.println("request greet #" + i + " -> " + await(eb.<String>request("greet", "dev" + i)).body()); System.out.println("publish news:"); eb.publish("news", "release 1.0"); Thread.sleep(200); for (String address : List.of("nobody", "fail")) { try { await(eb.request(address, "x")); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request " + address + " -> " + re.failureType() + " code=" + re.failureCode() + " message=" + re.getMessage()); } } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { await(eb.request("silent", "x", new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(300))); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> " + re.failureType() + " after " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } System.out.println("default request timeout: " + DeliveryOptions.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT + " ms"); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

The failures come back as NO_HANDLERS, RECIPIENT_FAILURE with code 42, and TIMEOUT after about 300 ms. With 1,000 ms the timeout simply arrives later: the consumer still never replies.

sections.h: The golden rule, the floor manager, and a back office that works in single file
sections.html:
Vert.x calls it the golden rule: don't block the event loop. Lesson 3 put it as the clerk who never stops to make a phone call. The Vert.x docs list what counts as a phone call: Thread.sleep(), waiting on a lock or a synchronized block, a long database operation, a complex calculation, spinning in a loop. They also give a budget. With one event loop and 10,000 HTTP requests a second, each request can take at most 0.1 ms.

Vert.x checks the rule for you, with a floor manager. A separate thread, vertx-blocked-thread-checker, walks past every event loop once a second. Each loop notes when its current task began, and the checker compares that with the clock. If a task has run for more than 2 seconds, it writes a warning in the log. Past 5 seconds, it adds the blocked thread's stack trace, the list of method calls the thread is inside. BlockedThreadDemo makes a clerk sleep for 6 seconds on an event loop:

[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2773 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 3772 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
...
io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked
	at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509)
	at workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo.lambda$main$0(BlockedThreadDemo.java:13)
	...
	at io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run(SingleThreadIoEventLoop.java:228)

The first warning came at 2.8 seconds, not 2.0, because the manager only walks past once a second. Search your logs for has been blocked for; the logger's name is io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker. And notice what the manager never does: interrupt. He writes it down and walks on, and the clerk stays on the phone.

The manager has one blind spot. He measures one task at a time, so ten 300 ms calls in a row hold a loop for 3 seconds and never produce a warning. Short blocking calls are the kind that never reach the logs.

For blocking work there's executeBlocking, the back office. It runs a Callable, a task that returns a value, on the worker pool, and completes a Future back on your context, so your own clerk writes the reply. ExecuteBlockingDemo tries it on an HTTP server with one event loop. Four requests arrive at once, and each needs a 500 ms lookup. The demo runs it three ways: blocking right on the loop, then executeBlocking with its default, then executeBlocking(callable, false). One run on a busy 4-core machine printed:

block-on-event-loop        4 requests x 500 ms -> 2201 ms, ran on [vert.x-eventloop-thread-0]
executeBlocking-ordered    4 requests x 500 ms -> 2012 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0]
executeBlocking-unordered  4 requests x 500 ms ->  511 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0, ..., vert.x-worker-thread-3]

The first line is the failure we expected: four lookups in a row on the clerk's own time. The second line is the surprise from the opening. The loop was free, so the floor manager had nothing to report, and yet the four lookups still ran one after another, all on vert.x-worker-thread-0. Twenty workers sat in the back office, and one of them did all the work.

The cause is one word in the docs: executeBlocking is ordered by default. Calls from the same context go into one queue and run in turn. Every request to one HTTP server shares that server's context, so every request joined the same queue. Pass false when the calls don't depend on each other, and they overlap: 511 ms, on four different workers.

Moving a call to the back office frees the clerk. Pass false, or the calls still wait in single file.

One last look at the back office itself. Its 20 threads are a bounded pool, like the ones in the executors track, so behind it you have a thread-per-request design again. That's fine, as long as you size it like one, with Little's law from lesson 1.

try.title: Three ways to make a slow call
steps: Open ExecuteBlockingDemo.java (or ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt). Predict the total time and the thread names for each of the three modes.
Run it with the command below.

Then run ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo and predict when the first warning appears and when the stack trace appears. Run it with -Pargs=2500 too: how many warnings now?

code.title: ExecuteBlockingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import io.vertx.core.http.HttpServer; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms blocking lookup. Three ways. */ public class ExecuteBlockingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String mode : List.of("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)); Callable<String> slowLookup = () -> { Thread.sleep(500); return Thread.currentThread().getName(); }; HttpServer server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler(req -> { switch (mode) { case "block-on-event-loop" -> { try { req.response().end(slowLookup.call()); // blocks the loop } catch (Exception e) { req.response().setStatusCode(500).end(); } } case "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); default -> vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup, false).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); } }).listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); java.net.http.HttpClient client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder() .proxy(java.net.http.HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.actualPort() + "/"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { calls.add(client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())); } Set<String> threads = new TreeSet<>(); for (var call : calls) threads.add(call.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body()); System.out.printf("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s%n", mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } }

alt.title: ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse import java.util.TreeSet import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.net.http.HttpClient as JdkHttpClient /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms blocking lookup. Three ways. */ fun main() { for (mode in listOf("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)) val slowLookup = Callable { Thread.sleep(500) Thread.currentThread().name } val server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler { req -> when (mode) { "block-on-event-loop" -> req.response().end(slowLookup.call()) // blocks the loop "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } else -> vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup, false).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } } }.listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() val client = JdkHttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(JdkHttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${server.actualPort()}/") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(4) { client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } val threads = TreeSet(calls.map { it.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body() }) println("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s".format(mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads)) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } }

try.expect: About 2,000 ms on the event loop thread, about 2,000 ms on one worker thread with the ordered default, and about 500 ms across four worker threads with false. Runs for this lesson measured 2,201, 2,012 and 511 ms, and later 2,408, 2,047 and 570 ms on a busier machine. The blocked-thread demo warns between 2 and 3 seconds in, once a second after that, and adds the VertxException: Thread blocked stack trace after 5 seconds. A 2,500 ms sleep gives zero or one warning, depending on when the checker happens to look.

refs.title: Vert.x 5.2.3 core documentation: The Golden Rule (source)

aside.title: Why would anyone want single file?
aside.html: Because order sometimes matters. Picture a desk that sends two jobs about the same parcel: first "mark it weighed", then "mark it shipped". If the back office ran both at once, the second could finish first and leave the record wrong. Ordered by default keeps the calls from one context in the order they were made, which is the safe choice when nobody has said otherwise. For independent lookups, like the price desk's, that safety only costs time, and false gives the time back.

compare.title: A desk that sends a blocking lookup to the back office

java.title: PriceDesk.java
java.html: public class PriceDesk extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("desk.price", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this desk's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(PriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));

kotlin.title: PriceDesk.kt
kotlin.html: class PriceDesk : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("desk.price") { msg -> val lookup = Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(lookup, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this desk's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::PriceDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

compare.note: Same Vert.x API, same threads at run time. Two Kotlin wrinkles came up while building this lesson's demos. vertx.deployVerticle({ PriceDesk() }, options) does not compile in Kotlin: Deployable is itself a single-method interface, so a bare lambda matches both overloads. Use a constructor reference (::PriceDesk) or Supplier { PriceDesk() }. And some Vert.x 5 signatures carry a @Nullable type annotation from vertx-codegen, which is not on the classpath, so Kotlin can fail with "Type annotation class 'io.vertx.codegen.annotations.Nullable' of the inferred type is inaccessible" when it infers a lambda's type. Giving the Callable and the lambda parameter explicit types, as above, avoids it. Java ignores the annotation.

worked.title: Unblock the price desk, step by step

steps.say: The price desk looks postage up in the price book, a database call that takes 300 ms, right on its clerk's time. It works in a demo with one request. Under load, every handler on the same event loop waits behind it, and the floor manager stays silent: he measures one task at a time, and each 300 ms lookup is under his 2-second limit.
steps.code: vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("desk.price", msg -> { try { msg.reply(PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())); // 300 ms on the event loop } catch (InterruptedException e) { msg.fail(500, "interrupted"); } });

alt.html: vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("desk.price") { msg -> msg.reply(PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())) // 300 ms on the event loop }

steps.say: First attempt: send the lookup to the back office with the default executeBlocking. The loop is free now, but six requests at once still take about 6 x 300 ms. They all come from this consumer's context, and the default is ordered.
steps.code: vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess(msg::reply);

alt.html: vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) }) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) }

steps.say: Second attempt: unordered. The lookups now overlap on the worker pool, and the replies still come back on the consumer's context. The lab's test checks both halves: under 1,000 ms in total for six lookups, and an event-loop lag under 150 ms.
steps.code: vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()), false) // independent calls .onSuccess(msg::reply) .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage()));

alt.html: vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) }, false) // independent calls .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) }

steps.say: Another design makes the limit visible: turn the whole desk into a worker verticle and deploy as many instances as you want lookups at once. Each instance takes one note at a time on the worker pool, so four instances means at most four lookups in flight, a number you can match to the database's connections.
steps.code: vertx.deployVerticle(BlockingPriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)); // at most 4 lookups at once

alt.html: vertx.deployVerticle(::BlockingPriceDesk, DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)) // at most 4 lookups at once

lab.title: Weigh parcels over the event bus, then unblock the price desk
steps: Run the tests. All five fail: WeighingDesk.start() throws, so the deployment in @BeforeEach fails.

Write WeighingDesk.start(): register a JsonObject consumer on ADDRESS, accept parcels up to LIMIT_KG with a reply {status, parcel, thread}, fail heavier ones with msg.fail(413, "too heavy"), and return the consumer's completion(). Four tests should pass.
Read priceLookupsDoNotBlockTheLoop. It makes its own Vertx with one event loop, sends six requests to the price desk, and measures both the event-loop lag and the total time.
Fix PriceDesk with executeBlocking. Try the one-argument version first and read the failure, then pass false.
hints: msg.body().getDouble("kg") reads the weight; Thread.currentThread().getName() gives the thread value.
msg.fail(413, "too heavy") reaches the requester as a ReplyException with failureType() RECIPIENT_FAILURE and failureCode() 413.

If a test times out after 30 seconds instead of failing fast, an assertion probably ran outside tc.verify(...). The test file writes @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout in full because JUnit's own @Timeout has the same simple name.
lab.done: All five tests in VerticleTest pass, and you have seen the ordered executeBlocking fail the total-time assertion.

drill.title: Write a desk that sends a blocking call to the back office
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a VerticleBase that answers requests on desk.price by running the blocking PriceBook.postageCents(parcel) off the event loop, in parallel across requests, and fails the message with code 500 on error. Then write the line that deploys two instances.

answer.html: public class PriceDesk extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("desk.price", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this desk's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(PriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));

alt.html: class PriceDesk : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("desk.price") { msg -> val lookup = Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(lookup, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this desk's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::PriceDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

recap: Vert.x runs on Netty event loops, two per core by default. A context ties your code to one thread, so a handler never runs at the same time as itself.
Vert.x 5 is futures only: asynchronous methods return Future, the callback versions are gone, and executeBlocking takes a Callable.
Each verticle instance is a desk with its own context: EVENT_LOOP (never block), WORKER (may block, still one task at a time) or VIRTUAL_THREAD (Java 21 or newer, await() parks).
The event bus offers send, request and publish on string addresses. A request fails with NO_HANDLERS, RECIPIENT_FAILURE or TIMEOUT (30 s by default), and delivery is best effort.
executeBlocking is ordered per context by default. Pass false for independent calls, or deploy a worker verticle with several instances.
The limit: the blocked-thread checker only reports, only after 2 s, and only one task at a time. Short blocking calls never reach the logs, so the golden rule stays yours to keep.

explain.prompt: A colleague wrapped four slow database calls in executeBlocking and is surprised that a burst of four requests still takes four times as long as one. Explain what a Vert.x context is, why their change didn't help, and what to do instead.
explain.answer: A context is where Vert.x runs a piece of code: a handler registered on a context always runs there, one task at a time, like a desk that always has the same clerk. All requests to one HTTP server share that server's context. executeBlocking moves the callable to the worker pool, the back office, which frees the event loop, but by default it is ordered per context: Vert.x queues calls from the same context and runs them one after another. So the four calls still ran in sequence, just on a worker thread instead of the event loop. If the calls are independent, pass false as the second argument so they run in parallel on the worker pool, or deploy a worker verticle with several instances to get a clear limit on how many run at once. Either way, size that parallelism to the database's connection pool behind it.

deeper.html:
Testing Vert.x code has its own traps, and the vertx-junit5 library exists because of them. A Vert.x callback runs on an event loop, after your test method has returned. If an assertion fails there, JUnit never sees it. The extension fixes that with VertxTestContext: the test passes only when you call completeNow() (or flag all checkpoints), and fails when you call failNow(...) or when an assertion inside tc.verify(() -> ...) throws.

This track's research ran the same failing assertion both ways. Outside verify, the test ran into the timeout after about 2.6 seconds with "The test execution timed out. Make sure your asynchronous code includes calls to either VertxTestContext#completeNow(), VertxTestContext#failNow() or Checkpoint#flag()", and the real AssertionFailedError was only printed to the log. Inside verify, it failed in 0.059 seconds with the actual assertion message. So every assertion in a callback goes inside verify, or inside tc.succeeding(...) and tc.failing(...), which wrap it for you.

Other details from the vertx-junit5 docs: the default timeout is 30 seconds, overridden per test with @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout (written in full, to avoid JUnit's @Timeout). A Vertx injected into a @BeforeAll method is shared by the class, one injected into @BeforeEach is shared by that test and its @AfterEach, and injected instances are closed for you. tc.checkpoint(n) gives a counter that must be flagged n times, handy for testing publish to several consumers. And in Vert.x 5, clients rely on Cleaner, the JDK's way to run cleanup when an object becomes unreachable, so a client object you stop referring to can close its pool while a test still uses it. Keep clients in fields during tests.

One trap belongs outside tests too: waiting for a result on the event loop itself, with future.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(). If the result needs that same loop to complete, the clerk waits for himself, and the call never returns. The test helpers in this lesson's lab call get only from the test's own thread, never from inside a handler.
